analysis.one_liner: Bans internet providers from blocking, throttling, or charging websites for faster delivery.
analysis.headline: A Republican net neutrality bill with a sponsor and 19 cosponsors never got a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee during the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes net neutrality rules into law: broadband providers could not block lawful websites or apps, slow down traffic on purpose, use non-harmful devices, or charge companies for faster delivery, and they would have to disclose their practices in plain language. Enforcement would happen through complaints to the Federal Communications Commission rather than broad regulations, and the bill would permanently classify broadband as a lightly regulated 'information service,' barring the FCC and state regulators from using other legal authorities to impose stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users, who would get legal guarantees that their provider cannot block lawful sites, slow their traffic, or charge websites a toll for faster delivery. Content, application, and device companies — including startups that cannot afford priority fees — would also benefit from guaranteed equal treatment on networks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and online content companies

how_it_helps.text: Bars broadband providers from blocking lawful content, applications, or services, subject to reasonable network management.
Bars providers from throttling — selectively slowing, speeding, degrading, or enhancing traffic based on source, destination, or content.
Prohibits paid prioritization, meaning a provider could not accept payment to speed up some internet traffic over other traffic.
Requires providers to publicly disclose, in plain language, their network management practices, performance, and commercial terms so consumers can make informed choices.
Bars providers from prohibiting the use of non-harmful devices on their networks.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband internet providers — cable, fiber, and wireless companies — would face binding conduct rules on how they manage and sell their networks. Indirectly, anyone who wanted stronger, utility-style regulation of broadband would give that up permanently, because the bill locks in the lighter-touch classification and strips backup regulatory authority.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is complaint-driven only: the FCC would handle violations case by case after harm occurs and is explicitly barred from adopting rules that expand the openness obligations beyond those listed in the bill.

The bill permanently classifies broadband as an information service and prohibits the FCC or state commissions from relying on Section 706 of the Telecommunications Act as a grant of authority, foreclosing the utility-style (Title II) regulatory approach favored by many consumer advocates and the House majority.

The bill preserves carve-outs — reasonable network management, emergency and law-enforcement needs, and 'specialized services' — that critics could argue leave room for providers to favor some traffic through exceptions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conduct rules are real and would give internet users protections that currently exist only at the discretion of the FCC. But the enforcement model is weak — complaints after the fact, no new rules — and the bill's central trade is codifying those protections in exchange for permanently locking in light-touch regulation and cutting off the stronger Title II approach. A supporter who favored utility-style regulation would fairly see this as a compromise that gives away future authority; a supporter who favored certainty without Title II would see it as the right balance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and received no markup, hearing, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress, dying in committee when the term ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 7, 2019 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The action history shows no further action — no committee vote, hearing, or floor consideration — after that referral for the remainder of the 116th Congress.
The bill had a Republican sponsor and 19 Republican cosponsors, all of them members of the House minority party.
The Energy and Commerce Committee was chaired by a Democrat in this Congress, and the bill's cosponsor list contained no members of the majority party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers came out ahead: no statutory blocking, throttling, or paid-prioritization rules were enacted, and the light-touch regulatory approach already in place through FCC rules remained untouched. Internet users got no enforceable statutory protections from either this bill or the Democratic alternative, neither of which became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, who kept light-touch rules

for.name: Greg Walden
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-OR); sponsor and former chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 7, 2019, a Republican-authored net neutrality framework codifying open-internet conduct rules while keeping broadband classified as an information service.

for.name: Broadband industry groups
for.what_they_did: Backed the information-service (Title I) approach to net neutrality over reclassification of broadband as a common-carrier service, favoring the framework this bill embodied.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which controlled the bill after referral, took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — over the full two-year Congress.

against.name: House Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Advanced its own stronger net neutrality bill reclassifying broadband under Title II (the Save the Internet Act, H.R. 1644, which passed the House in April 2019) rather than Walden's information-service approach.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 20 members — was a Republican, no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it, instead advancing its own Title II net neutrality bill that passed the House on a largely party-line vote in April 2019.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, fiber, and wireless carriers)
industries.note: The bill imposes conduct rules these companies opposed in their strongest form — no blocking, no throttling, no paid prioritization — but it also permanently locks broadband in as a lightly regulated information service and strips the Section 706 authority, foreclosing the utility-style regulation the industry fought for years to avoid. Consumers get binding conduct rules at the price of never getting the stronger regulatory framework.

industries.industry: Content, application, and device companies (edge providers, startups, streaming services)
industries.note: The bill guarantees them equal treatment on broadband networks — no blocking, throttling, or pay-to-play lanes — which protects small websites and startups that cannot afford priority fees. Ordinary users benefit from the same guarantee.

industries.industry: Online consumers and small businesses dependent on open internet access
industries.note: They would gain enforceable statutory protections against their provider favoring some traffic over theirs, plus plain-language disclosure of what they are buying.
